title: The opening greeting
hook: it begins with Ik Onkar and the Khalsa's greeting to Waheguru

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ardas, the standing prayer, and your line: stand and ask. Did you stand still for a breath before you began something? Today, the Ardas's very first words. Day six hundred twelve.

Two Sikhs meet at an airport, strangers, and one says: Waheguru ji ka Khalsa. The other answers right away: Waheguru ji ki fateh. They've never met, but in a handful of words they've placed each other. It's the Khalsa's greeting, which Sikh tradition traces to Guru Gobind Singh, and it's used at the start of a speech, the end of a letter, the top of a wedding card. Half of it, with one small symbol in front, is also how the Ardas begins. Before the prayer remembers anyone or asks for anything, it says who the victory belongs to. Today: the opening greeting.
screen: `TWO STRANGERS AT AN AIRPORT.` → `A FEW WORDS, AND THEY KNOW.` → `HOW THE ARDAS BEGINS.`

segments.voice: The Ardas opens: Ik Onkar, Waheguru ji ki fateh. Ik Onkar is the very first word of the Guru Granth Sahib: the numeral one joined to the sign for Onkar. One God, everywhere, flowing through everything. Then Waheguru, the wondrous Guru, a name for God. Ji is respect, like saying sir or dear. And fateh is victory. The grammar is worth a second look. Waheguru ji ki fateh doesn't quite say victory to Waheguru, like a cheer. It says the victory is Waheguru's: the victory belongs to God. In the full greeting the first half says the same thing about the community. Waheguru ji ka Khalsa: the Khalsa belongs to Waheguru. So the line often rendered victory to Waheguru carries the sense that the victory is already Waheguru's. The greeting hands everything over. The community isn't ours; it's God's. The victory isn't ours; it's God's. Two strangers at an airport have just reminded each other of that, in a handful of words. Putting it at the head of the Ardas does the same work. Whatever the prayer goes on to ask, a good marriage, a safe flight, a recovery, the first thing said is: if anything goes well, the victory is God's. That takes some weight off. It also takes some pride off. The same heading, Ik Onkar, Waheguru ji ki fateh, stands at the top of Guru Gobind Singh's Var Sri Bhagauti Ji Ki, where the Ardas's next lines come from. So the greeting is like the letterhead on a page: the first thing you see, telling you whose house you're in.
screen: `IK ONKAR: ONE, EVERYWHERE.` · `WAHEGURU JI: THE WONDROUS GURU.` · `FATEH: THE VICTORY IS GOD'S.` · `THE LETTERHEAD ON THE PAGE.` · then, large: `VICTORY TO WAHEGURU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say Ik Onkar, Waheguru ji ki fateh. Sit or stand comfortably. Let your breath settle. Then, slowly, say the words aloud or silently: Ik Onkar. Waheguru ji ki fateh. Say them a few times, unhurried. Each time, notice what you're handing over: whatever goes well today, the victory isn't yours to carry. If you don't pray, you can sit with the idea instead: a success that doesn't need your pride. The bell holds the time.
Fateh, victory. Ik Onkar, Waheguru ji ki fateh: one God everywhere, and the fateh belongs to the wondrous Guru.
Your line: victory to waheguru. When something goes well today, say the line once, and let the credit go. Day six hundred twelve.

howItsDone: The Ardas begins with Ik Onkar, Waheguru ji ki fateh, and Sikhs greet one another with Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki fateh, at meetings, in speeches and in letters.

myth: Waheguru ji ki fateh means the victory belongs to Waheguru
ki makes it possessive: the victory is God's.
the Ardas opens with a request

fork.setup: a stranger at the airport says to you: Waheguru ji ka Khalsa. what's the answer?
fork.reveal: the greeting has two halves: the Khalsa is Waheguru's, and the victory is Waheguru's. the second half also opens the Ardas.

original.note: Gurmukhi: fateh, victory; in Waheguru ji ki fateh, the victory belongs to God.

trapdoor: what you thought: Waheguru ji ki fateh is a cheer, like victory to God!
what it means: the victory already belongs to God; it hands the credit over.
what a scholar hears: ka and ki are possessive markers (ka for masculine Khalsa, ki for feminine fateh); the same formula heads Guru Gobind Singh's Var Sri Bhagauti Ji Ki.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): cut the superlative 'the name Sikhs use most for God' and the claim that the formula heads 'many' of Guru Gobind Singh's compositions (now: it heads the Var Sri Bhagauti Ji Ki, where the Ardas's next lines come from); the teach no longer says what all Sikhs mean or what the listener already knows.
Ardas opening as ੴ ਵਾਹਿਗੁਰੂ ਜੀ ਕੀ ਫ਼ਤਹਿ: confirm.
Claim that the formula heads many of Guru Gobind Singh's compositions in the Dasam Granth: confirm.
Grammar note (ka masculine, ki feminine, fateh feminine): confirm.

Reviewer: hook said the full greeting was five words (it is eight); changed to a handful of words. Teach now reconciles the carry (victory to waheguru) with the possessive reading. Origin of the greeting attributed to Guru Gobind Singh by tradition: confirm.
